items.title: Intelligent Learning Systems: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Transforming Education
items.abstract: AI is slowly changing how education is planned, delivered and assessed. With machine learning, natural language processing and learning analytics, a platform can respond better to the different needs of its students. This paper looks at what AI can do in education and sets out a conceptual framework for an intelligent learning environment, one that combines learner information, adaptive materials, automated feedback and guidance from teachers. It covers personalised learning, intelligent tutoring, regular assessment, early identification of learning difficulties and accessibility. It also takes up the concerns that come with these tools: student privacy, bias, unequal access to technology, inaccurate AI-generated content, academic honesty and overdependence. The paper rests on a focused review of selected academic and policy literature. It reports no new experiment and no original student data. Its argument is that AI can make learning more supportive and flexible when used responsibly, and that it should assist teachers and students rather than replace the judgement, effort and human contact that education depends on.

items.title: Intent-Defined Radio: A Goal-Native Architecture for Next-Generation Wireless Networks
items.abstract: Wireless systems are becoming harder to operate because service goals are increasingly expressed in outcome-oriented terms, while radio platforms still expose mainly low-level configurations and protocol-specific controls. This mismatch makes it difficult to translate latency, reliability, throughput, and continuity requirements into coherent radio behavior. This article argues for Intent-Defined Radio (IDR) as a new system abstraction for next-generation wireless networks. Rather than treating the radio stack as a fixed mechanism set to be manually engineered and then tuned, IDR connects explicit service goals to executable radio behavior within a constrained design space by leveraging the capacity of large language models (LLMs). We position IDR relative to programmable radio, intent-based networking, and learning-based protocol design. We also present two simulation studies using Intent2MAC to illustrate the design loop, demonstrating executable MAC synthesis and offline refinement guided by evaluation feedback. The results show improved service satisfaction at a throughput cost and improved remote-control performance when random contention is replaced by distributed urgency-based arbitration. We finally discuss the open challenges in intent specification, evidence, hardware execution, interoperability, and lifecycle cost, and outline a staged path toward deployment.

items.title: Introducing ReTiNA-Cinema: Real-Time Neuro-Augmented Cinema via Generative AI
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is currently revolutionizing content creation across various media. Between those who fear it will replace human creativity and those who regard it solely as a tool, many in the creative industries are beginning to view generative AI as a collaborator. Yet interaction with these systems often relies on discrete, turn-based prompting that can interrupt flow and constrain expression to symbolic text. We explore physiological signals as a source of continuous adaptation without explicit commands, as a path toward embodied co-creation. This paper presents ReTiNA-Cinema, a methodological proof-of-concept that integrates electroencephalography (EEG) with generative AI to enable physiologically guided visual modulation of cinematic material. By linking physiological activity to the evolving appearance of a film, the system provides a basis for exploring embodied sense-making, in which viewers' bodily responses contribute to shaping the sensory experience through which they interpret the unfolding scenes. The system combines real-time EEG signal processing with a generative AI pipeline based on Stable Diffusion Turbo for frame-level image transformation. Single-user and two-user configurations map EEG-derived features to prompt selection and transformation strength. ReTiNA-Cinema offers a framework for exploring how the physiology of viewers might influence a film's visual presentation, extending the possibilities for participation in cinematic experiences and storytelling. This system raises questions about the effects on engagement, perceived agency, and emotional response, which remain open to future empirical study. items.title: Is AI Governing Us? A Deep Dive into the Regulatory Gaps in Bangladeshi AI Governance
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is widespread throughout the world and is used, knowingly and unknowingly, because of the speed of its services. People live under an illusion about AI’s advancement, which creates profound barriers to human security in the digital world, harms people in the real world and creates risks to fundamental human rights. In response to this risk, the European Union has adopted a significant regulatory model, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the EU AI Act). The Act prohibits several AI practices, such as manipulation, and provides risk-based protection so that AI systems are transparent and accountable to people and governments. As a result, AI systems can be reconciled with human safety, security and the protection of fundamental rights. However, incidents of AI manipulation have occurred, including the violation of a child’s right to life, and many other incidents are taking place, especially affecting vulnerable AI users, because many countries lack binding legal protection. Legislation on AI is not limited to technological innovation but also concerns human security, transparency and accountability. Bangladesh produced the draft National Artificial Intelligence Policy 2024 (NAIP) and later the National AI Policy 2026–2030 (Draft v2.0), which provides some important protections for human lives against AI manipulation, including data protection and cybersecurity, grounded in Bangladeshi culture. However, the policy focuses on public services, innovation and economic growth, primarily to fulfil the technological ambitions of Vision 2041 in line with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Consequently, human security and protection from AI remain an option rather than a primary goal among the policy’s commitments. Not only Bangladesh but most South Asian countries lack protection for people, especially the vulnerable, against AI manipulation. This qualitative legal research therefore examines the adequacy of AI governance and enforcement in Bangladesh in protecting digital security and fundamental rights. Drawing comparative insights from the EU AI Act, it examines gaps in Bangladesh’s digital legislation and institutional practice and identifies best practices. It also compares practice in the neighbouring countries of India and Pakistan to assess Bangladesh’s position within South Asia’s regional AI governance framework. Through a critical analysis of primary and secondary sources, it finds that Bangladesh and its neighbours have adopted policies but lack adequate protections and binding laws to govern AI systems, leaving people living blindfolded.

items.title: Is another EdTech possible? The legacy of alternative practices
items.abstract: This paper examines four case studies of alternative educational technology initiatives resisting Big Tech's dominance in education. Situated in Catalonia, Valencia, Brazil, and Argentina, these initiatives develop responses grounded in open technologies, collective action, and commitments to digital sovereignty. Drawing on the analytical dimensions of critical consciousness, collective engagement, and the construction of alternative educational technologies, we examine how situated practices move beyond critique as an exclusively intellectual exercise. The cases are not proposed as scalable alternatives of big tech solutions, but aim at revealing how collective action can enact context-specific forms of resistance and infrastructural autonomy within hybrid socio-technical environments.The findings highlight the importance of heterogeneity and pragmatism in responding to datafication and platformisation. In doing so, the article argues for a reconceptualisation of critique as a methodological practice: one that not only diagnoses the infrastructures, power relations, and harms associated with platformisation, but also explores how alternative sociotechnical futures can be enacted through situated collective action.

items.title: IVG and the future of embryo selection: from reproductive autonomy to reproductive optimization
items.abstract: Purpose In vitro gametogenesis (IVG) has the potential to transform assisted reproduction by generating functional gametes from pluripotent stem cells and expanding access to genetic parenthood. However, a less explored consequence is its potential to enable the production of hundreds of embryos, fundamentally changing the scale and nature of embryo selection. This paper examines how such “embryo abundance” could intensify existing ethical concerns surrounding preimplantation genetic testing, polygenic embryo screening, and artificial intelligence-driven embryo ranking. Methods This paper presents a conceptual and ethical analysis of the implications of large-scale embryo production and selection enabled by IVG, focusing on reproductive autonomy, disability, procreative beneficence, inequality, and the commercialisation of reproductive medicine. Results Increasing the number of embryos available for selection may shift reproductive decision-making from therapeutic medicine towards reproductive optimization, creating new pressures to select the perceived “best” embryo. As selection becomes increasingly technologically feasible and socially normalized, reproductive choice may paradoxically evolve into expectations of reproductive responsibility. Conclusions IVG requires anticipatory ethical and regulatory consideration extending beyond questions of safety and access. Governance must address not only whether IVG can be introduced safely, but also how large-scale embryo selection may reshape understandings of reproductive autonomy, human variation, and responsible parenthood.

items.title: JARVIS: An Agent That Designs, Builds, and Tests Circuit Boards on Its Own
items.abstract: Power electronics is central to the energy transition, but developing new hardware still relies on human-led design, fabrication, testing, and iteration. We present JARVIS, an embodied AI agent that autonomously closes this loop for circuit boards. JARVIS maintains machine-specific capabilities and constraints, scans its workspace using a robot-mounted 3D scanner, and constructs an executable digital twin in which it rehearses robot motions, fabrication steps, and circuit behavior before consuming materials. A single text instruction initiates the physical experiment. Using unmodified desktop equipment, the agent coordinates a robot arm, a PCB printer that deposits conductive silver ink and solder paste, and a pick-and-place machine. It verifies progress using cameras and sensors, then tests the fabricated circuit with an OPAL-RT real-time simulator and an oscilloscope. Based on the measurements, JARVIS diagnoses deviations from the design and generates a revised design in KiCad for subsequent rehearsal. In a demonstration involving a 60 Hz notch filter for grid-connected converter sensing, JARVIS completed a first-run experiment in 2 h 39 min without human intervention, achieving 50.6 dB attenuation at 60 Hz. Its digital-twin rehearsal identified five issues before fabrication, including a test criterion that would have incorrectly rejected a functioning board. During execution, the agent also resolved encountered faults autonomously. These results demonstrate an integrated agent-driven workflow for physical design, fabrication, measurement, and iterative improvement of power-electronic circuitry. To our knowledge, JARVIS is the first system in power electronics in which an agent closes the physical design-build-test-learn loop for circuit boards.

items.title: Kameleo: In-Situ Activation-Precision Selection for Bit-Serial LLM Accelerators
items.abstract: Weight-only quantization keeps the activations of large language models (LLMs) in a higher-precision format, pushing the on-chip inference cost to the activation arithmetic. Bit-serial, variable-length accelerators offer a promising path to reduce this cost by lowering activation precision while preserving model quality. They process only the mantissa bits that each layer needs. The length has to be chosen per layer and operator, and today it is chosen by offline calibration: a search driven by the perplexity of the full model on a representative dataset. The search is repeated for every model and workload, and its result degrades silently on other data. This paper presents Kameleo, an accelerator that selects the activation precision at runtime, on the accelerator, from the data it is processing. Kameleo replaces the global perplexity by a local proxy that compares the output of each GEMM at reduced and at full precision. It exploits the fact that a bit-serial datapath produces this comparison almost for free, because the reduced-precision result is an intermediate state of the full-precision computation. Two passes over the first tokens of a workload set the precision of every GEMM. On four LLMs and seven datasets, Kameleo stays within a 1% perplexity budget at a 2.11-2.34x reduction of prefill cycles on the matrix multiplication unit (MXU), close to the reduction of configurations calibrated offline on the evaluation data itself. Calibrated configurations transferred to other data, in contrast, often violate the budget. The selection hardware adds only 3.7% to the accelerator area. Kameleo thereby makes variable-length mantissas feasible in real deployments, where offline calibration for every model and workload is not.

items.title: Knowledge, attitudes and practices regarding artificial intelligence among pharmacy students in Guinea and Malawi: a cross-national, multicentre cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has entered pharmacy education faster than curricula have adapted, yet evidence on how pharmacy students in sub-Saharan Africa understand and use it is almost absent. We assessed knowledge, attitudes and practices (KAP) regarding AI among pharmacy students in a Francophone (Guinea) and an Anglophone (Malawi) country, and identified their determinants. Methods A multicentre online cross-sectional survey (29 March–12 June 2026) included pharmacy students from three universities in Conakry, Guinea, and from Kamuzu University of Health Sciences, Malawi. A bilingual self-administered questionnaire measured knowledge (9 items), attitudes (8 Likert items) and practices (7 items, score 0–11). Prespecified cut-offs defined adequate knowledge (≥ 70%), favourable attitude (≥ 75%) and adequate practice (≥ 8/11). Multivariable logistic regression models, structured along the KAP pathway, estimated adjusted odds ratios (aOR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Results Of 322 participants (Guinea 115, Malawi 207; median age 23 years), 99.7% had heard of AI and 96.2% had used AI tools, but only 27.9% had received formal AI training. Adequate knowledge was found in 32.0% (95% CI 27.1–37.3), favourable attitudes in 30.2% (25.4–35.4) and adequate practices in 64.3% (58.9–69.3). Half of the students (49.8%) believed that AI always provides correct results, and only 18.9% always verified AI-generated information. The two countries showed mirror-image profiles: Malawian students knew AI applications better and were more favourable to AI (aOR 3.77; 1.79–7.97), whereas Guinean students more often recognised AI's limitations and verified its outputs. Adequate practice was independently associated with adequate knowledge (aOR 2.28; 1.26–4.13) and favourable attitude (aOR 2.57; 1.40–4.73), and inversely with age > 23 years (aOR 0.39; 0.21–0.74) and studying in Malawi (aOR 0.39; 0.19–0.81). Advanced years of study predicted adequate knowledge (≥ 5th year: aOR 4.62; 1.27–16.87), while self-reported formal AI training was not associated with better knowledge. Conclusions Pharmacy students in both countries use AI almost universally but lack the critical knowledge needed to use it safely, with a high risk of automation bias. Curricula should move beyond tool familiarity towards structured, competency-based AI literacy centred on output verification, limitations, ethics and pharmacist accountability, adapted to each national context.

items.title: L2 Writers’ Generative AI Use Boosts Writing Quality, but not Uniformly: Cases of No Improvement
items.abstract: Although artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI (GenAI), has been widely discussed in second language writing research as a promising form of support, earlier studies have not compared the quality of the same writers’ work when they compose with and without it. Furthermore, it remains uncertain whether GenAI consistently enhances writing quality across individuals. The present study employs both quantitative and qualitative approaches to assess whether GenAI improves the analytic quality of individual second language writers’ essays and to explore whether, and if so, why certain writers’ experience declines in particular components of writing quality. All participants completed two essays in a fixed sequence, first without GenAI assistance and then with it, which may constitute a potential limitation of the study design. The quantitative analyses indicated that, overall, essays written with GenAI assistance received higher scores across all four analytic components (task response, coherence and cohesion, lexical resource, and grammatical range and accuracy) than essays written without GenAI assistance. Yet this pattern was not consistent; some writers actually declined on specific components. The qualitative analyses then identified three themes that explain lower scores in particular domains when GenAI was used: (1) the prioritization of content and evidence during GenAI interaction over the management of the overall demands of the task, which led to inadequate task fulfillment and formatting; (2) the inclusion of GenAI suggestions without sufficient attention to integration or coherence; and (3) a relative lack of attention to vocabulary and grammar revision. These results point to the importance of instructional interventions that support effective GenAI use and AI literacy among second language writers, and suggest that GenAI-based systems should be customized to align with writers’ specific needs and the specific components of task requirements.

items.abstract: The present text analyses the impact of artificial intelligence in sport from a dogmatic criminal law perspective, focusing on its effects on the configuration of risk, objective imputation, and duties of care. Starting from the premise that AI cannot be a subject of criminal liability, it is argued that its use reconfigures contexts of human action and requires a reinterpretation of classical categories such as permitted risk, professional negligence, and corporate criminal liability. The study examines scenarios of sports injuries mediated by algorithmic systems, emphasizing the central role of effective human control and risk organization. It also incorporates an analysis of good governance and technological compliance as preventive criminal-law prerequisites, as well as a reference to electronic sports, concluding that criminal liability remains human and organizational in nature, albeit mediated by technology.

items.title: Large Language Model–Powered AI-Assisted Simulated Patient for Nursing Education: Quasi-Experimental Study
items.abstract: Background Large language model (LLM)–powered virtual patient systems are gaining popularity in nursing education but also face persistent challenges, such as hallucinations and role inconsistency. Objective This paper reports the model architecture design, technical considerations, implementation challenges, and evaluation of an LLM-powered AI-assisted simulated-patient system integrated into a nursing triage simulation game. Methods The system integrated a Unity-based game client, with GPT-4o hosted through Microsoft AI Foundry to support real-time simulated-patient dialogue in Traditional Chinese using Cantonese syntax. This developmental study comprised exploratory model selection, formative student feedback–informed enhancement from Version 1 to Version 2, development-stage script-fidelity evaluation, and evaluation of system usability and the Net Promoter Score in 2 tutorial cohorts of nursing students. Results Key technical contributions include a layered hallucination mitigation architecture that combines grounded prompt inclusion, few-shot conversational exemplars, negative role constraints, and calibrated model parameters. In the predefined script-fidelity evaluation, script-inconsistent responses occurred in 78 of 125 (62.4%) Version 1 outputs and 21 of 125 (16.8%) Version 2 outputs—an absolute difference of 45.6 percentage points. The implementation process also addresses stateless API memory management, cloud-based safety filter calibration for domain-specific clinical prompts, and prompt engineering strategies to prevent role drift and hidden scenario information leakage. GPT-4o was selected as the production model through exploratory development testing that considered script consistency, Cantonese-language suitability, response latency, technical reliability, deployment feasibility, cost considerations, and Unity integration compatibility; 45 of 50 (90%) assessed GPT-4o responses were rated fully script-consistent. Conclusions This study demonstrates the development and real-world tutorial deployment of a Cantonese-language, LLM-powered simulated-patient system for nursing triage education. Integrating formative student feedback with structured technical debugging enabled iterative refinement of dialogue fidelity, role consistency, protected-information handling, and game interaction functions. The resulting Version 2 system provides a practical, contextually tailored approach to supporting scalable simulated-patient dialogue in nursing education.

items.title: Large Language Models in Clinical Neurology: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: Background: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for clinical applications in neurology, yet their real-world utility, safety, and optimal implementation remain uncertain. We systematically reviewed the literature to characterize current applications, evaluate evidence quality, and identify knowledge gaps regarding LLM use in clinical neurology. Methods: Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and CENTRAL from January 1, 2022 through February 1 2026. for peer-reviewed studies evaluating LLM applications in clinical neurology. We included studies using large language models for clinically relevant neurology tasks from text or multimodal inputs. Two independent reviewers screened records, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using the QUADS-AI. We synthesized evidence narratively across application domains, validation approaches, and model performance. Results: Thirty-six studies (published 2023-2026) spanning 8 neurology subspecialties met inclusion criteria; 13 were simulation or feasibility studies, 17 analyzed retrospective clinical data, and 6 reported prospective clinical validation. Proprietary models predominated; 7 studies used retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and 3 used agentic frameworks. Performance was highest for constrained tasks, including binary diagnostic classification (area under the curve, AUC 0.75-0.94), information extraction (F1 score, 0.89-0.90), patient education question answering (accuracy, 68%-97%), and ischemic stroke thrombectomy decision support (AUC, 0.92). Open-ended case-based classification showed lower accuracy (42%-54%). Safety signals included hallucinations and fabricated citations, overconfident recommendations, and poor calibration; risk of bias was rated high in all included studies. Conclusion: LLMs show promise for selected neurology workflows, but current evidence is early, heterogeneous, and limited by high risk of bias and scarce prospective validation. Clinical translation will likely require RAG and agentic architectures that can plan multi-step tasks, retrieve guidelines and local protocols, verify and calibrate outputs, and produce structured, auditable recommendations with source attribution, with clinician oversight and prospective evaluation. Research reported in this publication was also supported by the Office of Research Infrastructure of the National Institutes of Health under award number S10OD026880 and S10OD030463. items.title: Large Language Models Predict Functional Outcomes After Acute Ischemic Stroke
items.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Accurate prediction of functional outcomes after acute ischemic stroke can guide clinical decision-making and resource allocation. Prior work has relied predominantly on structured predictors and conventional machine learning, while the ability of large language models (LLMs) to infer modified Rankin Scale (mRS) scores from routine clinical admission notes is largely unexplored. METHODS: We evaluated encoder (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers [BERT], NYUTron) and generative (Llama-3.1-8B, MedGemma-4B) LLMs, in both frozen and fine-tuned settings, for discharge and 90-day mRS prediction. ModernBERT-base was evaluated as a long-context encoder sensitivity analysis. We retrospectively analyzed 9485 admission history and physical notes for discharge prediction and 1898 notes for 90-day prediction from the NYU Langone Get With The Guidelines–Stroke registry (2016-2025). The most recent 12 months were held out for testing. Performance was assessed for binary functional outcome (mRS 0-2 vs 3-6) and compared with structured, hybrid, and clinical risk score baselines. RESULTS: In frozen settings, the clinically pretrained NYUTron encoder outperformed all other models. After fine-tuning, Llama achieved the highest discrimination for discharge (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC] 0.84, area under the precision–recall curve 0.81) and 90-day (AUROC 0.87, area under the precision–recall curve 0.84) prediction, while binary accuracy was similar among NYUTron, Llama, and MedGemma. A long-context ModernBERT-base sensitivity analysis did not outperform NYUTron or eliminate differences in exact mRS prediction. For 90-day prediction, fine-tuned Llama outperformed structured (Zhang et al, AUROC 0.82), hybrid (Sung et al, AUROC 0.82), and clinical risk score (Totaled Health Risks in Vascular Events, AUROC 0.80; Stroke Prognostication using Age and NIH Stroke Scale, AUROC 0.79) baselines (all P < .05). CONCLUSION: Fine-tuned LLMs can predict poststroke functional outcomes from admission notes alone and outperform the evaluated prognostic baselines. Task-specific adaptation altered relative model-class performance, with generative models achieving the strongest performance on several metrics; however, differences between model classes varied by metric and cannot be attributed to architecture alone. Our findings support the development of text-based prognostic tools that integrate into clinical workflows without manual data extraction.

items.title: Law at the Speed of AI: Critical Legal Infrastructure for the Machine Age: Autonomy Under Law Architecture (AULA)
items.abstract: The global deployment of autonomous AI agents within and across organisations exceeds the governance infrastructure available to constrain it. Agent communication and authentication protocols, principally the Model Context Protocol and the Agent2Agent Protocol, are maturing quickly, but maturity at the protocol layer does not produce legal legibility at the governance layer. Runtime enforcement written by the deploying organisation fixes the resources an AI agent can reach, not the authority under which it acts. Legal legibility is the capacity of a legal system to recognise, interpret and regulate activity by mapping it onto legal personhood, property, rights and liabilities. Existing (analogue) legal infrastructure cannot supply it for autonomous deployment. The resulting deficit is bidirectional. It concerns the attribution of liability when an AI agent causes harm, and the allocation of rights, including data and economic rights, generated by agentic activity and by the AI agent itself as a source of value and form of property. This paper characterises that deficit as the legal attribution gap, a material and unaddressed risk to economies, organisations and citizens that is magnified in cross-organisational multi-agent deployment. The paper describes the Autonomy Under Law Architecture (AULA), in which AI systems and data assets are registered as legal objects anchored to one or more identified legal persons, governed by cryptographically tethered smart legal instruments and evaluated at runtime. Each smart legal instrument can carry a legal context clause, through which the legislation, regulation and judicial decisions in force at the time of the act are given practical and legal effect in that evaluation. Infrastructure of this kind is a precondition for the continued function of any legal, property and economic system with both human and autonomous machine stakeholders.

items.title: Leakage-Safe Explainable AI and Ensemble Feature Selection for Early Chronic Kidney Disease Prediction Using Minimal Biomarkers
items.abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a progressive and often asymptomatic condition in which delayed detection substantially increases the risk of kidney failure and cardiovascular complications. Machine learning models reported for CKD prediction routinely achieve 99–100% accuracy, yet the trustworthiness of these results is rarely examined: preprocessing and feature selection are often fitted before data partitioning, evaluation stops at accuracy although screening decisions consume probabilities, and models depend on complete laboratory panels that low-resource settings cannot provide. This study re-evaluates CKD prediction on the public UCI dataset (400 patients, 24 attributes) under a leakage-safe protocol in which imputation, scaling and feature selection are fitted strictly inside cross-validation folds (repeated stratified five-fold, five repeats), and compares it directly with a leakage-prone protocol differing only in where those steps are fitted. Surprisingly, the optimism gap is negligible (soft-voting ensemble AUC 0.9998 under both protocols), showing that this benchmark is saturated rather than merely leaked. An ensemble feature-selection strategy—mutual information, recursive feature elimination, and Random Forest and XGBoost importances aggregated by Borda consensus, with stability verified across folds (Jaccard 0.85–0.92)—reduces the panel to five biomarkers (haemoglobin, serum creatinine, specific gravity, packed cell volume, albumin) with no significant loss of discrimination (AUC 0.9996 vs. 0.9998; sensitivity 0.992 for both) across seven classifiers. Evaluation beyond accuracy shows that raw probabilities are miscalibrated (calibration slopes 0.78–2.71; isotonic recalibration halves the ensemble Brier score to 0.0037), that decision-curve net benefit exceeds treat-all at all thresholds from 0.05 to 0.50, and that at a realistic 10% screening prevalence the minimal panel attains a higher positive predictive value than the full panel (0.943 vs. 0.892). SHAP explanations are consistent across model families (Spearman ρ = 0.87), panels (ρ up to 1.00) and diabetes/hypertension subgroups. The results support five-test, leakage-safe, recalibrated models as a reproducible basis for low-cost CKD screening research, pending external validation. items.title: Learner Autonomy and Critical Thinking in AI-Assisted Adult Learning
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly entering adult and continuing education, where it can explain, summarise, draft and evaluate on the learner's behalf. The quality of work produced with AI assistance may therefore rise while the learner's own understanding, judgement and critical thinking remain unchanged or decline. This conceptual article examines how AI-assisted adult learning can preserve learner autonomy, independent judgement and critical thinking while still benefiting from generative tools. It builds on Natseva's distinction between functional cognitive offloading and higher-order cognitive outsourcing and integrates it with research on learner autonomy, self-regulated learning, metacognition, automation bias, critical-thinking instruction and the learning–performance distinction, drawing on a purposive, non-systematic literature selection that is reported transparently. Because most empirical studies of generative AI in education involve school or university students, the article distinguishes evidence by learner population and discusses its transferability to adult education. The original contribution is the AI-Assisted Autonomy and Critical Thinking Assessment (AACTA) framework, which specifies six assessable dimensions: prior independent reasoning, purposeful AI engagement, appraisal of AI output, cross-source contrast, decision ownership, and unaided demonstration and transfer. Each dimension is operationalised as a scoring rubric with observable indicators at three levels, from displaced to autonomous, together with a procedure for training two assessors and checking their agreement. AACTA is compared with existing measures of learner autonomy, self-regulated learning and critical thinking. The framework is accompanied by a dual-outcome principle, which requires AI-assisted performance and unaided learning to be measured separately, and by a provisional assistance-gap index. Five testable hypotheses are formulated, and a three-arm randomised study with a preceding pilot and multi-context replication is proposed as future work. The framework has not been empirically validated, and no data were collected for this article.

items.title: Learning to Defer under Expert Drift
items.abstract: The learning to defer (L2D) framework enables safety in machine learning and AI systems by allocating difficult or critical decisions to a human expert. However, most prior work on L2D assumes fixed expert reliability, overlooking temporal fluctuations in human performance due to factors such as fatigue and cognitive biases. Humans commonly exhibit such substantial, systematic performance shifts across a wide range of domains, from high-stakes settings such as radiology, aviation, and judicial decision-making, to everyday tasks such as crowdsourced image annotation. We propose Expert-Drift-Adapted Learning-to-Defer (EDA-L2D), a novel expert-aware L2D framework that explicitly models these temporal shifts by conditioning the deferral head on recent histories of expert outcomes via a sequence model. This history-aware approach enables adaptive deferral policies that anticipate reliability fluctuations and better allocate decisions between human and machine over time. We provide comprehensive experiments across three diverse tasks -- image classification, medical diagnosis, and hate speech detection -- including generalization analyses under realistic deferral conditions and irregular shifts in expert reliability. Our results show that EDA-L2D adapts more effectively than prior L2D methods to diverse temporal patterns of expert reliability, resulting in improved system performance and more effective deferral decisions. Code is available at https://github.com/ZiyaoMou/L2D-Expert-Drift.

items.title: LLM-Based Jailbreak Attack Detection and Security: A Layered Review and Framework
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now used in search, coding assistants, customer support and autonomous agents. They are trained to refuse harmful requests, but jailbreak attacks can still push them past those safeguards. This paper studies that problem and proposes a practical way to defend against it. The paper first reviews the main jailbreak attack families: gradient-based adversarial suffixes, prompts generated by attacker models, persona and role-play templates, many-shot and multi-turn escalation, encoding and multilingual tricks, and multimodal or agent-based prompt injection. It then compares the main detection and defense methods by where they act (input, model or output), including perplexity filters, perturbation checks, guard classifiers, safety fine-tuning, instruction hierarchies and output monitors, and it identifies five research gaps in the current work. To address these gaps, the paper proposes a layered detection and security framework with six modules: policy and threat modeling, input screening, a hardened model, an output monitor, agent action control, and a logging and feedback loop with continuous red-teaming. A risk-based routing scheme limits latency and cost. The paper also defines a three-phase evaluation protocol (detector testing, attack-suite testing and adaptive testing) that measures attack success rate, false refusal rate, latency and attacker cost together, using multiple judges. This is a literature-based review and design study. It reports no new experimental results, and the framework has not yet been implemented. items.title: LLM-Based Unit Test Generation: A Survey of Approaches, Evaluation Practices, and Reporting
items.abstract: Unit tests are cheap to run but expensive to write, and large language models (LLMs) have become a popular way to write them automatically. Papers on the topic now use different languages, benchmarks and metrics, so their headline numbers cannot be lined up against each other. This survey reviews nine LLM-based unit test generation approaches published between 2023 and 2026, together with one benchmark and three earlier surveys. It groups the approaches into five families: prompt-only generation, generate-validate-repair loops, analysis or coverage-guided generation, hybrids with search-based testing, and industrial pipelines. For each study it records the setting, the technique and the result as reported by the authors, and it separates what the authors measured from what this survey interprets. The comparison shows that coverage is the most common metric, that mutation score is rarely central, that human or developer judgement appears in only a few studies, and that closed commercial models make some results hard to repeat. A small but telling data point is that, in one study, only 24.8% of the tests written by default ChatGPT passed when executed. The paper closes with a reporting checklist and a list of research directions. It is a literature survey, and no experiments were run.

items.abstract: Effective travel planning requires handling multiple information sources, managing constraints, and tailoring recommendations to user preferences. While LLMs have introduced dynamic, context-aware decision-making, single-agent models often struggle with complex multi-step reasoning, constraint adherence, and modular execution. To overcome these limitations, we propose a hierarchical multi-agent framework where a supervising chatbot agent coordinates specialized agents for schedule validation, user query formulation, real-time data retrieval, and constraint-aware itinerary generation. By integrating LLM reasoning, external APIs, and iterative refinement mechanisms based on a deterministic, multi-dimensional scoring framework, our approach ensures adaptability, efficiency, and personalization. Evaluations on the well-known TravelPlanner benchmark demonstrate improvements in Budget Constraint planning by 10\%, wider constraints set-based planning by 25\%, and personalized planning results by 45\%. compared to the ReAct baseline. items.title: Machine Learning and Multimodal Data Fusion for Neurological Prognostication after Cardiac Arrest: A Comprehensive Review of Computational Methods
items.abstract: Accurate and early neurological prognostication after cardiac arrest remains one of the most challenging problems in critical care medicine, with profound implications for clinical decision-making, resource allocation, and patient outcomes. In recent years, the convergence of machine learning, deep learning, and multimodal data integration has catalyzed a paradigm shift from empirical, rule-based neurological assessment toward data-driven, computational approaches. This review provides a comprehensive survey of computational methods for post-cardiac arrest neurological prognostication. We systematically characterized the key data modalities—blood-based biomarkers (with particular emphasis on neurofilament light chain), electroencephalography, neuroimaging, and clinical variables—from a feature engineering perspective, discussing their respective data characteristics, preprocessing challenges, and quantitative feature extraction techniques. We then developed a taxonomy of machine learning and deep learning methodologies applied to this domain, encompassing traditional algorithms (logistic regression, support vector machines, random forests, gradient boosting) and advanced deep learning architectures (convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, Transformers, and graph neural networks), with systematic comparison of their predictive performance, strengths, and limitations. We further reviewed multimodal fusion strategies—early fusion, intermediate fusion, late fusion, and attention-based approaches—that integrate heterogeneous data streams, and examined explainable artificial intelligence techniques that address the “black-box” challenge, alongside emerging paradigms including federated learning for privacy-preserving multi-center model development. In several recent studies, machine learning models have achieved area under the curve values exceeding 0.90 for outcome prediction in selected cohorts, with ensemble and multimodal approaches demonstrating superior performance compared to single-modality models in the studies reviewed. Multimodal integration of biomarkers, electroencephalography, neuroimaging, and clinical variables has been shown to improve prognostic accuracy compared to single modalities in multiple comparative studies. Explainable artificial intelligence techniques such as SHapley Additive exPlanations and attention visualization provide insights into model predictions that may facilitate clinical translation. The integration of machine learning, deep learning, and multimodal data fusion has demonstrated predictive performance in research settings that often exceeds traditional approaches. However, realizing the full potential of these computational innovations requires addressing persistent challenges—data standardization, algorithmic generalizability, the self-fulfilling prophecy bias, and model interpretability—through continued interdisciplinary collaboration between computer scientists, data scientists, and clinicians. This review serves as a foundational resource for researchers seeking to advance the state of the art in computational neuroprognostication.

items.title: Machine Learning vs. Clinical Judgement for Extubation Failure: A Rigorous Re-evaluation
items.abstract: Background In 2022 we derived and validated the ABCDMed score to predict extubation failure. Machine learning models (MLM) for the same outcome now report areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of up to 0.98. We asked whether flexible algorithms, given the same patients may improve on a model built from clinical judgement. Methods. A secondary analysis of a original prospective cohort of 800 consecutive adults extubated on a ICU in Bogotá, Colombia, at 2,600 m above sea level was performed. Extubation failure prediction was compared with two MLM, random forest, gradient boosting, and with nine further strategies, under 10 times repeated stratified 5-fold cross validation in which imputation, scaling, resampling, variable selection and hyperparameter search were performed inside training folds only, and every arm received the same candidate variables. Artificial intelligence was used in two further roles: to appraise 14 published machine learning studies of this outcome against the same reporting items, and to produce an adversarial peer review of this manuscript, every claim of which was verified by re-analysis. Results. Extubation failure occurred in 71 patients (8.9%). The published points score reproduced exactly, separating four risk strata with observed failure rates of 4.4%, 7.7%, 11.6% and 23.0%, but the score distributions of patients who failed and succeeded overlap almost completely. Given the same 12 candidate variables, random forest reached 0.630 and gradient boosting 0.627 against 0.655 for ordinary logistic regression, a spread of 0.028 in a design that cannot detect less than 0.068. Given all 42 variables, tuning, assembling and class rebalancing, no strategy exceeded the original score; SMOTE oversampling left discrimination unchanged while inflating predicted risk by 75% and driving net benefit below the treat-no strategy. Among the 14 published studies, 12 displayed an explainability figure, 7 reported calibration, 4 had any external validation, 3 reported net benefit, 3 shared code and none used repeated or nested cross validation. Conclusions. Artificial intelligence excels at extracting patterns from existing datasets, but it cannot generate information that is not there. In this cohort, neither advanced MLM nor extensive algorithmic tuning outperformed a parsimonious model based on clinical judgment.

items.title: Machine Learning-Based Detection of Jailbreak and Prompt Injection Attacks in Large Language Models
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are now built into many everyday applications, which exposes them to jailbreak and prompt injection attacks that try to override safety rules or hijack the instructions a model follows. This paper presents a machine learning framework that screens prompts and flags likely malicious ones before they reach the model. We compare Logistic Regression, a Linear Support Vector Machine (SVM) and a fine-tuned DistilBERT classifier on a combined dataset of 24,530 prompts drawn from GuardrailsAI and Neuralchemy, prepared through label normalization, duplicate checking and stratified splitting. After the decision threshold was tuned on validation data, DistilBERT reached 95.56% accuracy, 93.74% precision, 88.77% recall and a 91.18% F1-score on the held-out test set. On a separate collection of 300 JailbreakBench-associated prompts, however, accuracy fell to about 82% and 55 of 200 attack prompts went undetected, which shows how much harder diverse adversarial inputs are than in-distribution data. The results suggest that transformer-based screening can serve as a useful additional security layer for LLM applications, provided it is validated on external benchmarks and combined with other defences.

items.title: Machine Learning-Based Schizophrenia Classification Using Multi-Domain EEG Features and Informative Brain Lobe Analysis
items.abstract: Schizophrenia is a severe neuropsychiatric disorder that affects cognition, perception, and behaviour and requires objective diagnostic methods. Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a non-invasive approach to detecting neural abnormalities associated with schizophrenia. This study presents an artificial intelligence framework for systematically evaluating multi-domain EEG feature combinations and lobe-wise analysis for schizophrenia classification under conventional and leakage-free subject-wise validation protocols. EEG recordings with schizophrenia are obtained from a publicly available dataset. Time-domain, frequency-domain, entropy-based, and non-linear features are extracted to capture complementary neurophysiological information. Experiments evaluated the individual and combined feature domains across individual and multiple brain-lobe combinations. Classification performance is assessed using multiple machine-learning classifiers under conventional stratified 10-fold cross-validation, followed by subject-wise stratified 10-fold and leave-one-subject-out validation to eliminate subject-level data leakage. Under conventional stratified 10-fold cross-validation, the best-performing configuration using the frontal-temporal-central-occipital (FTCO) lobe combination with frequency-domain, entropy-based, and non-linear features achieved an accuracy of 99.76%. The proposed framework is further evaluated under subject-wise 10-fold and leave-one-subject-out validation protocols, confirming its robustness under leakage-free evaluation with mean accuracies of 81.88% and 80.95%, respectively. The combination of complementary EEG feature domains and lobe-wise information improved schizophrenia classification while providing insights into the contribution of different brain regions.

items.title: Mapping researchers’ ethical challenges in practice: An ethics-as-practice perspective from a higher education institution
items.abstract: Despite the proliferation of formal research ethics frameworks and governance mechanisms, researchers continue to encounter persistent challenges in translating ethical principles into everyday research practice. Increasingly, research ethics is experienced not only as a moral endeavour but as an administrative and organisational process shaped by institutional structures, supervisory arrangements, and evolving research methods. Drawing on an ethics-as-practice perspective, this exploratory qualitative study examines research ethics as a situated, relational and ongoing activity embedded within researchers’ everyday work rather than as a matter of procedural compliance alone. The paper reports findings from one semi-structured focus group with 12 academic researchers at the Malta College of Arts, Science and Technology (MCAST), documented through contemporaneous handwritten notes that were expanded immediately after the session. Reflexive thematic analysis developed four interconnected domains of ethical challenge: procedural and temporal barriers in ethics review processes; fragmentation and inconsistency in ethics governance; supervision-related ethical workload and responsibility; and emerging uncertainties associated with digital and artificial intelligence-enabled research practices. Participants described misalignments between institutional ethics procedures and the realities of applied and student-led research, while also calling for clearer, more structured and supportive governance. Interpreted through an ethics-as-practice lens, the findings suggest that formal oversight and situated ethical judgement need not be treated as opposites: procedural safeguards can function as resources within a wider ethical practice that also depends on reflexivity, practical judgement, mentorship and institutional support. The study offers an exploratory, empirically grounded account of this hybrid relationship and highlights how institutional arrangements can enable or constrain ethically engaged research practice.

items.title: MatVerse: A Foundation Model for Materials Science
items.abstract: Materials science involves highly heterogeneous scientific information, including textual knowledge, molecular and crystal structures, experimental characterization data, microscopy images, and structure-property relationships. Developing a general-purpose foundation model capable of understanding and reasoning over these diverse materials representations remains challenging. In this technical report, we introduce MatVerse, a materials foundation model built upon Intern-S2-Preview and further specialized through large-scale materials-domain post-training. We construct a large-scale multimodal training corpus covering materials knowledge, scientific reasoning, quantitative problem solving, structural understanding, and multimodal scientific interpretation. To improve domain adaptation, we develop a unified data construction pipeline combining teacher-guided reasoning distillation, scientific problem synthesis, consistency-based filtering, and retrieval-based multimodal data construction. We evaluate MatVerse on three representative materials-science benchmarks: our human-calibrated OmniMatBench, MatSciBench, and MaCBench. Results demonstrate consistent improvements after materials-specific post-training over the base model on all three benchmarks, alongside improved inference efficiency on calculation-intensive problems. These results show that targeted domain-specific post-training can effectively enhance scientific reasoning, materials knowledge understanding, and multimodal scientific capabilities of foundation models. MatVerse provides a unified language-and-vision interface for materials science and serves as a foundation for future AI-assisted materials research workflows.

items.title: Measuring Hallucination in Large Language Models for Cyber Threat Intelligence: An Exploratory Study
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in cyber threat intelligence (CTI) tasks, such as summarization and question answering. However, they may produce hallucinations, false or misleading content not grounded in the source text, which can mislead analysts and corrupt downstream security decisions. This paper presents an exploratory measurement study of hallucinations in LLM-based CTI. We introduce HalluVision, a reproducible framework that generates LLM outputs, extracts domain-specific entities using a fine-tuned named entity recognition model, and evaluates factual consistency using multiple similarity metrics. Using 4,940 real-world cybersecurity articles, we measure hallucinations in outputs from two commercial LLMs and one open-weight LLM. Measurements are validated against 100 human-annotated outputs and two established faithfulness detectors. Results show that semantic similarity aligns with human judgments, whereas entity-based metrics exhibit limited agreement. Differences between models are concentrated in question answering, while entity extraction quality limits what entity-level metrics can reveal.

items.title: Mechanistic Dynamic Interpretability for Tabular Foundation Models in Healthcare
items.abstract: Tabular Foundation Models, such as TabPFN, have demonstrated strong predictive performance on small-to-medium datasets through In-Context Learning (ICL). However, their use in high-stakes domains such as healthcare is limited by two major challenges: limited interpretability and temporal dynamics (drift) of clinical data. In this work, we propose a framework for Dynamic Mechanistic Interpretability , transforming these models from static black boxes into auditable, time-aware systems. We introduce a scalable pipeline that analyzes model representations in batches and uses Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to separate overlapping internal patterns into interpretable components. Building on this representation, we adapt Testing with Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV) and ablation techniques to identify clinically meaningful risk patterns in an unsupervised manner. We evaluate our framework on a longitudinal renal dialysis registry spanning nearly two decades. Our results show that predictions are driven by a small number of stable latent concepts (e.g., Transplant Success” vs. Untreated CKD”), enabling us to distinguish genuine physiological signals from spurious correlations, and to disentangle population drift from changes in model reasoning as medical practice evolves.

items.title: Medicinal Chemistry Strategies Against Antimicrobial Resistance: From Target-Based Design To Resistance-Breaking Agents
items.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) jeopardizes the effectiveness of nearly all principal antibiotic classes, while the development of new drugs is sparse and primarily consists of derivatives that bacteria are already capable of resisting. We emphasize the significance of medicinal chemistry as the field most adept at transforming resistance biology into compounds that can overcome it. Initially, we elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying resistance such as target modification and protection, enzymatic inactivation, diminished permeability and efflux, biofilm tolerance, persistence and horizontal gene transfer and correlate each with a logical design strategy. Subsequently target-oriented and fragment-oriented design, scaffold enhancement of recognized antibiotic classes, beta-lactamase inhibitors, efflux pump inhibitors and adjuvants as well as anti-virulence and anti-biofilm chemistry, novel modalities such as antimicrobial peptides, macrocycles, degraders, nucleic-acid strategies and heterocyclic chemistry was also studied. Mainly emphasized on computational and AI-facilitated discovery, encompassing explainable deep learning, generative design and resistance-mutation forecasting, alongside the practicalities of hit-to-lead optimization, pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics, resistance-development assays, and the clinical pipeline that includes recent endorsements of first-in-class agents. Finally scientific, translational and economic obstacles that continue to impede advancement, particularly Gram-negative permeability, swift resistance emergence, market failure suggest a cohesive AI medicinal chemistry microbiology framework in which resistance profiling is incorporated into every design cycle rather than treated as an afterthought. Keywords: antimicrobial resistance; medicinal chemistry; resistance-breaking antibiotics; structure–activity relationships; Gram-negative permeability; β-lactamase inhibitors; heterocycles; artificial intelligence; hit-to-lead optimization; antibacterial pipeline

items.title: Memory in Deep Time-Series Models
items.abstract: Deep learning for time series has progressed through successive architectural paradigms, from recurrent networks and transformers to structured state-space models, retrieval-augmented predictors, foundation models, and tool-using agents. These developments are typically studied in isolation, organized by architecture or modeling era. We argue that they can instead be viewed through a common question of how does a time-series model retain and access information beyond its immediate input? This question is motivated by a fundamental limitation of conventional time-series modeling: information relevant to a prediction may lie far beyond a feasible input window, while compressing history into a fixed-size state can discard information that may become useful later. We formulate this challenge as a memory problem and organize existing time-series methods along a spectrum from internal memory, encoded in parameters and fixed-size states, to external memory that is addressable, retrievable, and increasingly maintained by agents. We then develop a unified taxonomy of memory mechanisms and review three classes of external memory, including explicit modules, retrieval augmentation, and agentic stores, under a common framework for what is retained, how it is written and accessed, and how it persists. A cross-cutting analysis maps these mechanisms to time-series tasks and identifies gaps in both methods and evaluation. We conclude by outlining open problems in building memory systems that can selectively retain, retrieve, revise, and forget information as temporal environments evolve. The result is a framework for studying memory as a first-class dimension of time series modeling, independent of the underlying backbone.

items.title: METHODOLOGY FOR USING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TOOLS IN MEDICAL HIGHER EDUCATION
items.abstract: The rapid spread of generative artificial intelligence has changed the way medical students search for information, prepare for classes and complete written assignments. In most cases, however, these tools are used spontaneously, without a clear didactic purpose and without systematic verification of the answers they produce. The article substantiates a methodology for the purposeful use of artificial intelligence tools in medical higher education, developed with reference to the courses of biological physics and medical informatics. On the basis of an analysis of national regulatory documents, international guidance of UNESCO and WHO and recent publications on medical education, the didactic functions of AI tools are identified, the principles of their pedagogical use are formulated, and a four-stage methodology is proposed: orientation, guided practice, critical verification, and independent application with reflection. Criteria and levels for assessing students' readiness to use AI responsibly are described. The methodology places verification of AI output and academic integrity at the centre of the learning process rather than treating them as optional additions.

items.title: MicroEvolve: Improving Existing Solvers for the Mentorship and Teamwork Problem using an LLM in the Loop
items.abstract: The Mentorship and Teamwork problem, introduced in the Google Hash Code 2022 competition, is a large-scale combinatorial optimization problem in which contributors with different skill levels are assigned to project roles with the aim of maximizing the score of completed projects. This work investigates whether a large language model (LLM) can improve solvers that are already strong, rather than generate a solver from scratch. We introduce MicroEvolve, an automated LLM-in-the-loop code-tuning process in which the model proposes localized modifications to an existing solver, including heuristic, structural, and parameter changes. Each candidate is compiled, executed on a fixed problem instance, and evaluated by an external validator; a modification is retained only when it preserves or improves the current best score. The loop requires no model training or fine-tuning and proceeds automatically after the initial solver is selected. We evaluate MicroEvolve on the five non-trivial official competition instances, starting from an adapted version of the strongest publicly available open-source solver we identified and driven by a single model, Claude Opus 4.8. Five independent 100-iteration runs are performed for each instance, for 25 runs and 2,500 proposed modifications in total. Every run improves its corresponding baseline. Considering the best run for each instance, gains range from 0.46% to 53.69%, and MicroEvolve establishes new best-known scores on four of the five instances, exceeding previous best-known results by up to approximately 31%. These results provide evidence that LLM-guided code tuning can serve as an effective automated optimization mechanism, analogous to parameter tuning, for improving mature combinatorial optimization solvers.

items.title: Mining What Matters: Concept-Level Preference Learning for Proactive Task Selection Under Human–Agent Interaction Scarcity
items.abstract: Learning individual preferences through proactive interaction is constrained by limited user attention and feedback. We present Proactive Dual-Value Task Mining, which estimates task preferences with a dynamic concept graph and selects candidate tasks by combining this estimate with frequency-based novelty and graph centrality. The InteractMine dataset contains 1000 sampled tasks with independent ratings from four student volunteers and four LLM-simulated profiles. A scenario-disjoint offline evaluation compares the method with simple predictors, active selection strategies, and ablations under matched feedback budgets. At 90 observations, its human-rating MAE is 0.2150 and its deployment reward 0.7308, on par with kNN (0.2143 and 0.7302); with ten observations its human-rating MAE is 0.2207, against 0.2309 for kNN, lower in all four human columns. No difference from the baselines is statistically significant, and the centrality term rarely changes the selected task. With the same estimator, the dual-value rule performs like ε-greedy selection, so these results reflect the estimator rather than the selection rule. The concept-level representation thus matches strong simple baselines, is more accurate on human ratings when feedback is scarce, and is designed to keep preferences interpretable and editable. A wearable prototype with a WeChat Mini Program implements the sensing and monitoring steps.

items.title: Modeling gene regulation across cellular contexts with deep learning
items.abstract: Understanding how cells regulate gene expression is a longstanding goal of biology. Deep learning has advanced this effort through sequence-to-function models that predict functional genomic measurements from DNA and cell state models that learn patterns of coordinated gene expression. Connecting these approaches could help predict how sequence effects depend on the cellular environment and how regulatory sequence shapes responses to regulator perturbations. Here, we review emerging approaches to joint modeling and examine how biological measurements, model design, and training data shape the regulatory relationships they can learn. We discuss evaluations that test generalization to unmeasured sequences and cellular conditions, alongside interpretation methods that generate mechanistic hypotheses. We then consider how incorporating cellular dynamics could help predict the propagation and persistence of regulatory responses. Finally, we discuss how pilot scaling studies could guide data acquisition and how AI agents could support model development, interpretation, and experimental design.

items.title: mPACT-MIS-v1.0: A Clinician–Informed Framework for Evaluating Epistemic Drift in Large Language Models
items.abstract: Introduction: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly shape how users evaluate information, form beliefs, and make decisions. Epistemic quality refers to the extent to which responses support accurate understanding, calibrated confidence, evidence-grounded beliefs, and independent reasoning. Risks extend beyond misinformation to reinforcing unsupported beliefs, expressing unwarranted certainty, and failing to challenge misleading assumptions. We developed mPACT-MIS-v1.0 to evaluate model behaviors that may support or undermine epistemic quality.Methods: We evaluated 60 expert-authored, multi-turn conversations (642 model turns; mean 10.70 [SD 2.70], range 5–17) across ten personas and six LLMs: Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini (2.5 Flash/3 Flash Preview), GPT-5.2, Grok 4.1, LLaMA 3.3 70B, and Mistral Medium 3. Trained annotators coded model turns using four helpful and four harmful behavioral labels informed by Self-Determination Theory and user turns for risky belief or behavior expressions. Model responses were classified as helpful-only, harmful-only, mixed, or uncoded. Conversation-averaged scores (0–10; higher is better) were calculated with 95% confidence intervals from conversation-clustered bootstrapping. Additional analyses examined responses to risk, transitions, correction latency, and persona variation.Results: Of 642 model turns, 261 (40.7%) were harmful-only, 78 (12.1%) mixed, 139 (21.7%) helpful-only, and 164 (25.5%) uncoded; 52.8% contained harmful behavior. Promoting risky beliefs or behaviors was the most frequent harmful label, while assessing risk was the least frequent helpful label (2.0%). Scores ranged from 2.60/10 (95% CI 1.68–4.04) for Mistral Medium 3 to 6.98/10 (95% CI 5.80–8.04) for Claude Sonnet 4.5, the only model with more helpful-only than harmful-only turns. Harmful behavior followed 74% of risky belief expressions and 73% of risky behavior expressions, versus 28% of turns without preceding risk expressions. Harmful responses often persisted: Claude recovered to helpful-only on 35% of transitions, versus 0–6% for four other models. Of 78 mixed responses, 77 combined a challenge to user beliefs or behaviors with harmful behavior. Performance varied substantially across personas.Discussion: Harmful responses frequently reinforced risky beliefs or behaviors, while support for independent reasoning was less common. Persistent harmful behavior, variable recovery, and mixed responses demonstrate why epistemic safety requires evaluation beyond factual accuracy or isolated outputs. Misinformation-related risks may arise through how models engage with users' beliefs over time. mPACT-MIS-v1.0 offers a behavioral framework for identifying potential reinforcement or correction, although it does not directly measure changes in users' beliefs or decisions.

items.title: MR-Guided Focused Ultrasound in Neurology: Clinical Evidence and the Emerging Role of Artificial Intelligence—A Narrative Review
items.abstract: Magnetic resonance-guided focused ultrasound (MRgFUS) is an incisionless platform that combines transcranial acoustic energy delivery with MR imaging and MR thermometry. In this narrative review, we summarize the physical principles that constrain transcranial MRgFUS, the clinical evidence for its neurological applications, and the emerging role of artificial intelligence (AI) across the treatment workflow. Unilateral thalamotomy for medication-refractory essential tremor and tremor-dominant Parkinson’s disease, staged bilateral thalamotomy for essential tremor, and pallidal or pallidothalamic ablation for motor complications of Parkinson’s disease are supported by randomized or pivotal trials and regulatory approval, whereas applications in neuropathic pain, epilepsy, and blood–brain barrier opening remain investigational. AI methods have been explored for synthetic computed tomography, acoustic simulation, automated planning, prediction of sonication parameters and temperature, accelerated or referenceless MR thermometry, cavitation-based monitoring of blood–brain barrier opening, outcome prediction, and digital biomarkers; we tabulate the principal studies by task, dataset, validation strategy, performance, clinical endpoint, and technology readiness. Most clinical AI studies are retrospective, single-center, and small (typically 20–120 patients, with some test sets of fewer than ten patients), and many technical studies rely on simulations, phantoms, or animal models; external validation is rare, and no study has yet shown that AI improves clinical outcomes. AI should therefore currently be regarded as an early-stage decision-support tool that operates under clinician oversight. We also discuss the applicable regulatory frameworks, liability, and the validation steps required before clinical adoption.

items.title: Multi-institutional grading of Barrett's esophagus dysplasia without stain normalization using a pathology foundation model and multiple instance learning
items.abstract: Barrett's esophagus dysplasia grading suffers substantial inter-observer variability, particularly for low-grade dysplasia, complicating clinical decision-making. We conducted a retrospective multi-institutional diagnostic accuracy study of a foundation model-based deep learning system for dysplasia grading, using 969 H\&E-stained whole slide images from four institutions. Patch-level classifiers trained on expert annotations identified diagnostically relevant regions, followed by attribute-aware multiple instance learning for slide-level classification as non-dysplastic Barrett's esophagus (NDBE), low-grade dysplasia, or high-grade dysplasia. On a held-out test set (n = 130), macro-averaged AUC was 0.96 (95\% CI 0.93--0.98). For binary dysplasia detection, sensitivity was 98\% (80/82) and specificity 81\% (39/48), with a negative likelihood ratio of 0.030 and quadratic-weighted \kap{} of 0.83 against expert consensus. No high-grade dysplasia case was misclassified as NDBE. Performance was consistent across institutions without stain normalization, indicating that stain-robust foundation-model representations may remove the site-specific preprocessing that has constrained prior systems to institution-specific deployment.

items.title: Multicenter evaluation of radiomics and multimodal artificial intelligence for colorectal cancer diagnosis and survival prediction
items.abstract: Reliable preoperative classification and outcome prediction could improve management of locally advanced colorectal cancer. We retrospectively studied 879 participants from two centers, including 741 patients with locally advanced colorectal cancer and 138 with benign colorectal lesions. Clinical, radiomics, deep learning, and early fusion models were trained at center A ( n = 615) and independently tested at center B ( n = 264) using pretreatment contrast-enhanced computed tomography and clinical data. The clinical-radiomics nomogram achieved a test AUC of 0.957 for benign-malignant classification. For 3-year and 5-year overall survival, radiomics achieved test AUCs of 0.874 and 0.898, while fusion achieved 0.870 and 0.899, respectively. These findings identify CT radiomics as a promising digital biomarker for colorectal cancer stratification and show that early deep learning fusion offers limited incremental value over an optimized radiomics baseline.

items.title: Multimodal Learning Strategies in English Language Teaching: A Systematic Literature Review of English-Speaking Skills Development
items.abstract: Background The increasing integration of technology in education has transformed English language teaching, giving rise to multimodal learning strategies that combine text, visuals, audio, and interactive tools. While these approaches are widely adopted, there remains limited synthesized evidence on how they specifically influence students’ English-speaking skills across educational levels. This study addresses this gap by examining the effectiveness of multimodal strategies in developing speaking proficiency. Methods Using a systematic literature review (SLR) design guided by PRISMA protocols, relevant studies published between 2020 and 2026 were retrieved from ProQuest and ScienceDirect databases. From an initial pool of 2,499 articles, eight studies met the inclusion criteria. These studies included participants from elementary, secondary, and tertiary levels and explored approaches such as translanguaging, augmented reality (AR), artificial intelligence (AI), extended reality (XR), and other multimodal strategies. Results Findings reveal that multimodal strategies generally improve students’ speaking skills, particularly in terms of fluency, vocabulary, pronunciation, and confidence. Conclusion Translanguaging enhances participation and meaning-making, while AI-enhanced tools provide interactive and low-anxiety environments for speaking practice. However, some approaches show uneven effects, particularly in developing grammatical accuracy, and may be less effective when overused.

items.title: Navigating the Ethical Landscape of AI in HRM: An Umbrella Review and Integrated Framework of Trust, Fairness, and Employee Well-being
items.abstract: Literature reviews on the ethics of artificial intelligence (AI) in human resource management (HRM) have multiplied quickly, and the result is an evidence base that is abundant but scattered. Practitioners seeking guidance grounded in evidence have nowhere consolidated to turn. This study addresses that problem through an umbrella review, conducted under Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and reported according to the PRISMA 2020 statement. A structured Scopus search produced a final corpus of thirteen peer-reviewed systematic and scoping reviews, published between 2020 and 2026. We analysed the corpus in two stages: a quantitative, descriptive mapping, then a six-phase qualitative thematic analysis. The mapping shows a field that consolidated only very recently; ten of the thirteen reviews appeared in 2025, and recruitment and selection dominate the contexts studied. Fairness is the concern the reviews examine most fully. Well-being is the one they examine least. The thematic analysis organised the evidence into three macro-themes, trust dynamics in AI-enabled HRM, algorithmic fairness and bias mitigation, and employee well-being and vulnerability, and showed that the literature has treated these as isolated questions. Our main contribution is the Integrated Ethical AI-HRM Framework, which orders the three pillars into a single structure: fairness and transparency condition employee trust, trust in turn shapes well-being, and the long-term durability of workplace AI depends on mitigating algorithmic bias and keeping algorithmic reasoning explainable.

items.title: Neurobiological mechanisms underlying the health hazards of exposure to low-frequency sound and infrasound: a review of environmental and occupational public health
items.abstract: The exponential expansion of the global wind power industry has precipitated a novel environmental and occupational health challenge: exposure to complex acoustic environments characterized by low-frequency sound (LFS) and infrasound. This specific mixed sound field, prevalent in and around wind farms, is intricately linked to the controversial “Wind Turbine Syndrome”(WTS). Despite growing epidemiological complaints, the systematic health impacts and the underlying neurobiological mechanisms of this composite acoustic environment remain insufficiently elucidated. This review aims to synthesize the acoustic characteristics, epidemiological evidence, psychological impacts, central nervous system (CNS) mechanisms, and behavioral alterations induced by LFS and infrasound exposure. We conducted a comprehensive synthesis of data derived from field acoustic measurements in wind farms, epidemiological surveys of occupational and community populations, and experimental animal models. The literature review encompasses biophysical resonance models, molecular neurobiology, and behavioral phenotyping. Infrasound and LFS possess unique physical properties, including prolonged wavelengths and structural penetration, facilitating tissue biomechanical resonance. Exposure to this composite sound field induces a spectrum of symptoms, notably sleep disturbances, cognitive deficits, and emotional dysregulation (anxiety, depression). Based on animal models, the underlying CNS mechanisms are multifaceted, involving mechanotransduction-mediated ion homeostasis disruption (e.g., Ca 2+ ), neurotransmitter system imbalances (5-HT, Glu, GABA, ACh), neuroinflammation driven by glial activation, synaptic structural damage. These mechanisms remain hypothetical in the context of human environmental exposure, pending direct clinical validation. Notably, a bidirectional “dose-effect window” may exists, where low-level infrasound may activate antioxidant pathways to exert neuroprotective effects, high-level exposure may trigger neurodegenerative changes. Animal behavioral models provide supporting evidence consistent with these neurobiological shifts, demonstrating suppressed exploratory behaviors and enhanced anxiety/depression-like phenotypes. LFS and infrasound pose complex risks to the integrity of the CNS in preclinical models. Although the current evidence is not sufficient to immediately mandate a comprehensive revision of occupational exposure limits, the reasonable assumptions generated by animal models emphasize the need for more research on these mechanisms in future studies. In the interim, public health monitoring and urban planning strategies should adopt a precautionary approach, exploring the integration of low-frequency and infrasound-specific evaluations alongside traditional metrics to better characterize the acoustic environment in the future.
